name: Wendy Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Paybridge, a payroll software company with about forty people, on the second floor above a furniture shop on Mill Road. I look after the timesheet and holiday-pay part of our system, which is old PHP code, PHP being the language a lot of websites were built in fifteen years ago. Most mornings I'm fixing tickets, which are bug reports from customers, like a care home whose night shifts are adding up wrong. I'm slow, honestly, and I know it, because I only did a two-year diploma and half the code is older than my time there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a customer's payslips finally come out right and I know a nurse somewhere gets paid properly on Friday. What wears me out is Gareth, my team lead, asking why I don't just use the AI assistant like everyone else. I don't use it, I never have, and I'm tired of explaining that. Rosa, my girlfriend, works in home care and earns less than me, so between us there's about three weeks of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, probably in the group chat with Priya from support. I'd say the tools were mostly a way for bosses to squeeze more tickets out of the same people. Online I'd share a few articles about how much power those data centres used for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't make my life easy just because AI flops. Paybridge let five people go last spring, and that wasn't AI, it was a lost contract with a hospital group. I'm the slowest developer on my team, there are only two other software firms in this town, and I have less than a month of money saved. So hype or no hype, I still lie awake some nights doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try to get faster at the old code, maybe by doing the PHP course my diploma tutor recommended. I'd put fifty a month into savings even if it means fewer takeaways with Rosa. And I'd finally join the tech workers' union branch that a guy from the other firm keeps emailing about, because layoffs happen with or without robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to the normal knot in my stomach. It's like a storm missing your town but your roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said layoffs happen with or without AI. Who do you think decides that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, and the investors behind them. When we lost the hospital contract, nobody asked us whether to cut people or cut the owner's bonus. I'm not saying they're evil, but the people at the bottom always go first, and right now that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine parts of your day could even a weak AI take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boring tickets, probably, like resetting a customer's holiday year or rewriting the same report query. Those are maybe a third of my week. If Gareth gave those to a tool, I'd have less easy work to hide my slowness behind, which sounds silly but it's true.

say: I'd say **I told you so** about the AI hype in our team group chat.
I'd call the tools a way for **bosses to squeeze** more tickets from the same staff.
think: Even if AI flops, Paybridge **cut five people** last spring over a lost contract.
I'm the **slowest developer** on my team, with few other firms in town.
I have **under a month** of money saved, so I still worry about rent.
do: Take the **PHP course** my diploma tutor recommended to speed up on old code.
Put **fifty a month** into savings, cutting some takeaways with Rosa.
Join the **tech workers' union** branch that keeps emailing me.
feel: Brief **relief**, then the usual **knot** about money and layoffs.
S0.quote: Paybridge let five people go last spring, and that wasn't AI, it was a lost contract with a hospital group.
fieldNote: Her worry **predates AI**: thin savings, few local firms and a recent layoff round.
She sees the **routine third** of her week as a cover for being slow.
Blames **owners and investors** rather than the technology itself.

steps.text: Keep fixing timesheet tickets and take the tutor's PHP course
Save fifty a month by cutting weekly takeaways
Join the local tech workers' union branch this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Here's the next one. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd keep my head down, because Gareth would be all for it. Online I'd be loud: I'd post that companies are using AI to get rid of juniors and keep the savings. I'd say there should be rules, like a company has to give notice and retraining money before it swaps people for software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding is right there on the list you just read, and so are checking and answering customers, which is basically my whole job. A junior who doesn't use the tools and is slower than the tools is the first name on the spreadsheet. I think I'd be gone within a year or two, and there's nothing like this job within an hour's bus ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop pretending and look at public sector jobs, like IT support at the council or the hospital, where unions are stronger and things move slower. I'd cut our streaming and the gym, which is about forty a month. I'd push the union branch to ask Paybridge for a written promise on retraining before any cuts. And I'd write to our local councillor, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like being picked last at school, except it's rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use the AI tools. In this world, would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the boring tickets, if Gareth made it a rule. But I don't want to train the thing that replaces me by feeding it my fixes. I know that sounds stubborn, and Rosa says it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Rosa talk about the night you heard about cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we could keep the flat on her wage alone, and we couldn't, not for long. Rosa would say we'd manage, because she always says that. Then she'd go quiet and start looking at her rota for extra shifts, and I'd hate that most.

say: I'd post that firms use **AI to cut juniors** and keep the savings.
I'd call for **rules on notice** and retraining money before staff are replaced.
think: Coding, checking and answering customers are **my whole job** in this picture.
A slow junior who avoids the tools is **first on the list**, likely within two years.
do: Apply for **council or hospital IT** jobs where unions are stronger.
Cut **streaming and gym**, saving about forty a month.
Write to our **local councillor** about protecting junior workers.
feel: Slightly **sick**, like being **picked last** with rent at stake.
S1.quote: A junior who doesn't use the tools and is slower than the tools is the first name on the spreadsheet.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** within two years, which drives the alarm.
Refuses AI partly on **principle**: she won't train her own replacement.
Her biggest pain is **Rosa taking extra shifts** to cover for her.

steps.text: Apply for IT support jobs at the council and hospital
Cancel streaming and the gym to save forty a month
Ask the union branch to demand a written retraining promise
Write to the local councillor about notice rules for AI layoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that nobody voted for. I'd be at whatever protest there was outside the town hall, and I'd tell everyone who'd listen that the government needs to pay people while this happens. I wouldn't be polite about it online either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished as a developer by 2028, and so would most of my team. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me, because there's nothing hands-on about what I do. I don't have savings, I don't have a degree, and I don't have a plan for something this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign on for unemployment benefit the week the job went, no pride about it. We'd move somewhere cheaper, maybe back to my mum's spare room if Rosa could stand it. I might try to get into home care with Rosa. Home care lasts until around 2031. That's three years, which isn't a career, it's a waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest gets tight just saying it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said home care is a waiting room. Would you still do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because a waiting room with a wage is better than the street. But I'd be doing it knowing the robots come for Rosa's job and mine at the same time. That's the part I can't think past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to cut one thing first, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat. Rent is eight hundred of our money every month and there's nothing else that big. Everything else is crumbs, like phone contracts and bus passes.

say: I'd call it a **disaster nobody voted for** and join any town hall protest.
I'd demand the **government pays people** while the change happens.
think: I'd be **finished as a developer** by 2028, along with most of my team.
Robots arriving later **doesn't help me**, because my work has no hands-on part.
do: Sign on for **unemployment benefit** the week the job goes.
Move to my **mum's spare room** to drop the eight-hundred rent.
Try **home care work** with Rosa until robots arrive around 2031.
feel: **Panicky**, with a **tight chest** just saying it aloud.
S2.quote: Home care lasts until around 2031. That's three years, which isn't a career, it's a waiting room.
fieldNote: No savings, no degree and **no plan**: she is overwhelmed rather than strategic.
Sees the three-year robot gap as **a waiting room**, not a way out.
Cutting the **flat** is her only big lever.

steps.text: Claim unemployment benefit the week the Paybridge job ends
Move into mum's spare room with Rosa to drop the rent
Train for home care work alongside Rosa
Join protests at the town hall for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is close to the last. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: I'd say it needs rules and a safety net, and I'd say it louder because there'd be time to act. I'd tell the union branch this is our five years to get something in writing. I'd probably be the annoying one at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but it's still fast for me. I'm slow at learning new things, I know that about myself. I'd spend the first two years hoping it wasn't true, which is exactly the wrong thing to do, and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a night course in something hands-on in the first year, probably electrical installation at the college on Station Road, because robots come around 2034. I'd keep my Paybridge job as long as it lasted to pay for it. I'd save whatever we could, even if it's only thirty a month. And I'd keep pushing the union to bargain for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with a bit of ground under my feet. Five years is enough to fail at one thing and try another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend two years hoping. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone like me get cut. I don't move for warnings, I move for faces. If Danny, the other junior, got let go, I'd sign up for the course the next morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work, rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Carlos is an electrician and he's never been out of work. It's real, it's physical, and you can see if it's done right. I'd be thirty-two when I finished, which isn't too old to start again.

say: I'd say it needs **rules** and a **safety net**, and say it louder with time.
I'd tell the union branch these are **our five years** to win terms.
think: **Five years** still feels fast because I'm a **slow learner**.
I'd waste the first two years **hoping** it isn't real.
do: Start an **electrical installation** night course at the Station Road college.
Keep the **Paybridge job** as long as possible to pay for it.
Save **thirty a month** and push the union for retraining money.
feel: **Scared**, but with **some ground** under my feet.
S3.quote: I don't move for warnings, I move for faces.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose developer work**, just later.
Admits she **moves for faces**, not warnings: change needs a visible trigger.
Her uncle the **electrician** is her model of safe work.

steps.text: Enrol in the electrical installation night course on Station Road
Save thirty a month while still paid by Paybridge
Push the union branch to bargain for retraining funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the final one. The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have ten years to get this right, so no excuses. I'd want laws on how firms can replace people, and a proper public retraining fund. I'd probably share that line a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like enough time to let myself off the hook, and that worries me. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives, which is young enough to restart but old enough to be tired. The end point's the same, so I'd still lose this job, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see if it was actually coming, because I always do. Then I'd start the electrical course part-time, around year three, while still at Paybridge. I'd stay in the union and maybe stand as branch rep. I'd vote for whoever promised the retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It's a slow worry instead of a fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years lets you off the hook. What would you say to yourself at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say I started early, not that I waited for Danny to get fired. Rosa would tell me to stop planning and just book the course. She's usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything for you and Rosa beyond work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd stop putting off a cheaper place in the next town over, where we could actually save. I keep saying next year. Ten years would make next year easier to say again, which is the trap.

say: I'd say **ten years** means **no excuses** for leaders.
I'd push for **laws on replacement** and a public retraining fund.
think: Ten years lets me **off the hook**, and that worries me.
At **thirty-seven** I'd still lose this job, just later.
do: Wait **a year or two** before acting, as I usually do.
Start the **electrical course** part-time around year three.
Stand as **union branch rep** and vote for a retraining fund.
feel: A **slow worry** rather than a fast one.
S4.quote: Ten years would make next year easier to say again, which is the trap.
fieldNote: She names her own **delay habit** as the main risk.
Still expects to **lose the job**, which keeps her anxious, not calm.
Politics and **union work** stay central in every picture.

steps.text: Watch for a year or two before changing anything at Paybridge
Start the part-time electrical course around year three
Stand for union branch rep at the tech workers' branch
Vote for candidates promising a public retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. There's no time to be slow in it, and slow is what I am. What would help is money while you retrain, real money, not a voucher, and a rule that firms give six months' notice before replacing people with software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I don't use the AI tools. It's not just fear. I think a lot of it was built on other people's work without asking them, and I don't want my name on that. My girlfriend Rosa says principles don't pay rent, and she's right, but they're still mine.

headlineQuote: My girlfriend Rosa says principles don't pay rent, and she's right, but they're still mine.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old junior developer** at a small payroll software firm, with under a month saved.
She **never uses AI tools**, partly from fear and partly from principle about how they were built.
Her worry **starts before AI**: a recent layoff round, few local firms and a thin cushion.
She blames **owners and investors** and turns to unions, councillors and protest in every picture.
Her plan B is **electrical work** like her uncle, but she admits she waits too long.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time for a slow learner to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: **Real money** while retraining and six months' **notice** before AI replacement.
